diagrams.name: inst-p382-curette-parts
diagrams.title: Parts of the working end (front view, universal curette)

labels.answer: Set 3: 11/12 posterior mesial, 13/14 posterior distal; anterior/premolar all surfaces

cloze.text: The area-specific explorer (#11/12) has a {{c1::long complex}} shank with the tip at a {{c2::right angle}} to the lower shank, and paired working ends.
The #11/12 explorer is used to explore {{c1::healthy sulci and deep periodontal pockets}}.
The Orban (#17) explorer is {{c1::single-ended}} with the tip at a right angle to the lower shank; it is mainly used on {{c2::anteriors}}.
cloze.extra: Good adaptation is needed on curved surfaces.

cloze.text: The pigtail explorer has a {{c1::curved}} shank and paired working ends; it is best for hard deposits and exploring healthy sulci, because its tip {{c2::cannot reach deep pockets}}.
The periodontal probe detects {{c1::bleeding on probing (BOP)}} and {{c2::suppuration (pus)}}.
With the periodontal probe, hard deposits and roughness are detected in conjunction with the {{c1::explorer}}.
The periodontal probe evaluates the health of the periodontium by measuring {{c1::pocket depth}}.
The periodontal probe measures gingival recession, overgrowth and {{c1::clinical attachment levels (CAL)}}.
Measured with a probe: overjet is the {{c1::horizontal}} dimension; overbite is the {{c2::vertical}} dimension.
Besides periodontal measurements, the probe is used to measure the size of {{c1::intraoral and extraoral lesions}}.
The 6 probing sites per tooth are distofacial, facial, mesiofacial, distolingual, lingual and mesiolingual; at each site the {{c1::deepest}} reading is recorded.
Probing uses the {{c1::assessment}} stroke: light strokes with {{c2::no lateral pressure}}.
Once the probe is inserted into the pocket, the working end is kept {{c1::parallel to the root surface}}.
The probing walking stroke is a series of small bobbing strokes {{c1::1 to 2 mm}} apart.
cloze.extra: Stop at each point and take a measurement.

cloze.text: When probing, gently press down until the probe tip touches the {{c1::junctional epithelium}}.
At interproximal contacts, tilt the probe slightly ({{c1::about 10°}}) into the {{c2::col}}.
Probing depths are recorded to the {{c1::nearest full millimeter}}.
Probe design: a {{c1::blunt}} tip calibrated in millimeter markings; cross-section can be {{c2::circular or rectangular}}.
Marquis probe: markings at {{c1::3-6-9-12 mm}}, with black bands at {{c2::3–6 mm and 9–12 mm}}.
Williams probe: markings at {{c1::1-2-3-5-7-8-9-10 mm}} — it omits the {{c2::4 mm and 6 mm}} markings.
Michigan O probe: markings at {{c1::3-6-8 mm}}.
UNC 12 (or 15) probe: marked every mm to 12 (or 15); black bands at {{c1::4–5 mm, 9–10 mm (and 14–15 mm)}}; commonly used for {{c2::comprehensive periodontal charting}}.
WHO probe: a {{c1::0.5 mm ball tip}} and a color band from {{c2::3.5 to 5.5 mm}} (markings 3.5, 5.5, 8.5, 11.5 mm); primarily used for {{c3::Periodontal Screening and Recording (PSR)}}.
Goldman Fox probe: a {{c1::flat (beavertail)}} tip design; markings 1-2-3-5-7-8-9-10 mm (omits 4 and 6 mm, like the Williams).
Novatech probe (markings 3, 6, 9, 12 mm): designed with a {{c1::right-angle bend}} for easier access to {{c2::posterior teeth}}.
Naber's probe: double-ended, paired mirror-image curved working ends marked at {{c1::3 mm intervals}}; used specifically to assess {{c2::furcations}}.
Florida probe: a {{c1::computerized}} probing system that measures to the {{c2::tenth of a millimeter}}; more accurate because of {{c3::consistently applied force}} and precise depth measurement.
The choice of instrument for calculus removal is based on the {{c1::size}} and {{c2::location}} of the deposits.
Sickle scalers are used on {{c1::large}} deposits located {{c2::supragingivally}}.
{{c1::Universal curettes and rigid-shank area-specific curettes}} are used for {{c2::medium}}-sized supra- and subgingival deposits.
For small deposits, {{c1::universal curettes}} are used supragingivally and on the {{c2::cervical third}} of the root.
Small deposits on the {{c1::middle or apical third}} of the root are removed with {{c2::area-specific curettes}}.
Sickle scalers are designed to remove {{c1::medium- to large-sized supragingival}} calculus deposits.
cloze.extra: Some sources indicate use 1–2 mm subgingivally.

cloze.text: The {{c1::universal curette}} is the most versatile removal instrument, used both supra- and subgingivally.
Area-specific curettes are used supra- and subgingivally for {{c1::precise root debridement}}.
A universal curette has {{c1::two parallel}} cutting edges per working end.
A sickle scaler has a {{c1::pointed}} back and toe; universal and area-specific curettes have a {{c2::rounded}} back and toe.
In cross-section, a sickle scaler is {{c1::triangular}}; universal and area-specific curettes are {{c2::half-moon (semicircular)}}.
Sickle scalers, universal curettes and area-specific curettes all come with {{c1::straight or complex}} shanks.
Sickle scaler shanks are {{c1::strong and rigid}} for heavy deposits; curettes (universal and area-specific) have {{c2::longer}} shanks for root access.
A universal curette with a standard shank is for {{c1::light}} calculus; a rigid (thicker) shank is for {{c2::moderate-to-heavy/tenacious}} calculus.
The face of a sickle scaler and of a universal curette is at {{c1::90°}} (perpendicular) to the terminal shank.
With a universal curette, the lower shank must be {{c1::tilted toward the tooth}} to obtain correct angulation.
The face of an area-specific curette is angled at {{c1::60°–70°}} to the terminal (lower) shank, so correct angulation is achieved when the {{c2::lower shank is parallel to the tooth surface}}.
The anterior sickle scaler is for {{c1::anterior sextants}}: straight shank, single or paired working ends.
The universal sickle scaler can treat {{c1::all surfaces}} — efficient if time is limited.
Before standard curette use, larger calculus can be prepared with {{c1::powered instruments or files}}.
Area-specific curettes have {{c1::paired, mirror-imaged}} working ends (matched sets, e.g., #11/12, #13/14); the most popular examples are {{c2::Gracey}} curettes.
The Gracey curette series was developed in the {{c1::1940s}} by Dr. Clayton Gracey (University of Michigan) with {{c2::Hugo Friedman}}, founder of Hu-Friedy.
Gracey {{c1::1/2 and 3/4}} are used on anterior teeth only (all surfaces).
cloze.extra: Set 1: "the First Numbers" — they clean everything at the front.

cloze.text: Gracey 5/6: anteriors and premolars all surfaces; molars only the {{c1::facial, lingual and mesial}} surfaces.
cloze.extra: Set 2 (5/6, 7/8, 9/10) are "the middle numbers": anteriors, premolars and the F/L of molars.

cloze.text: Gracey {{c1::7/8 and 9/10}}: anteriors and premolars all surfaces; posterior teeth {{c2::facial and lingual}} surfaces.
Gracey 11/12: anteriors {{c1::mesial and distal}}; premolars and posteriors {{c2::facial, lingual and mesial}} surfaces.
cloze.extra: Set 3 (11/12 & 13/14): "the Classic M/D Pair", usable in all areas of the mouth.

cloze.text: Gracey 13/14: anteriors mesial and distal; posterior teeth {{c1::distal}} surfaces.
Gracey {{c1::15/16}} is used on posterior teeth only — facial, lingual and mesial surfaces.
Gracey {{c1::17/18}} is used on posterior teeth only — distal surfaces.
Specialized instruments are ideal for {{c1::deep pockets, furcations and complex root anatomy}}.
Vision instruments: the working end is shortened by {{c1::half}}.
{{c1::O'Hehir and DeMarco}} curets have tiny circular discs at the working end — useful for {{c2::furcations}}.
Diamond-coated files: the working end is covered with fine diamond grit and has {{c1::no cutting edges}} (e.g., diamond-coated Naber's furcation probes).
Diamond-coated files are used with {{c1::light}} pressure and are ideal for furcation areas and {{c2::fine finishing of root surfaces after debridement}}.
After Five curette: blade width {{c1::10%}} narrower than standard; available in standard or rigid shanks; {{c2::decreases tissue distention}}.
cloze.extra: Specialized curettes are compared to standard curettes unless noted; terminology such as "after five" can depend on the brand.

cloze.text: "After Five" curettes are designed for periodontal pockets {{c1::deeper than 5 mm}}.
Mini-Five curette: like the After Five (3 mm longer terminal shank, 10% narrower blade) but with a blade {{c1::50% shorter}}; standard or rigid.
Mini-Five curettes are great for {{c1::concavities, depressions and root surfaces within furcations}}, and narrow, deep pockets.
Micro-Mini Five curette: blade width {{c1::20%}} narrower than the Mini-Five; blade length 50% shorter; shank {{c2::more rigid}} than the Mini-Five.
Micro-Mini Five curettes are great for very deep {{c1::tenacious}} calculus, {{c2::tight}} tissue and deep or narrow pockets, narrow furcations, depressions, line angles and fine deposit removal.
The hoe removes {{c1::heavy, bulky supragingival}} calculus and is especially effective on the {{c2::lingual surfaces of mandibular anteriors}}.
Both the hoe and the file are used with {{c1::vertical pull}} strokes.
cloze.extra: File: adapt the entire face against the deposit.

cloze.text: The file is used to {{c1::crush}} calculus in preparation for removal with other instruments, especially on {{c2::burnished}} areas.
A file can be used when {{c1::powered instruments}} are contraindicated or unavailable.
Besides calculus, a file can be used to smooth {{c1::overhangs}}.
Files are helpful in deep, narrow pockets because of their {{c1::small size and flat working end}}, but can {{c2::stretch the tissue excessively}}.
File design: a series of {{c1::fine short blades}} on the side of the head, and a {{c2::rounded}} back to facilitate subgingival insertion.
The file's thick shank gives strength but limits {{c1::tactile sensitivity}}.
Avoid {{c1::metal}} instruments when scaling titanium implants; however, a {{c2::metal probe}} used gently is acceptable around implants.
cloze.extra: Evidence supports the use of non-metal instruments.

cloze.text: Alternatives to metal curettes for implants include {{c1::plastic}}, {{c2::graphite}}, Teflon-coated, gold-coated, titanium-coated and solid titanium alloy instruments.
Plastic implant instruments can leave {{c1::debris}}; many textbooks still suggest plastic, but research is still developing.
Use only {{c1::light lateral pressure}} on implants, because calculus on and around implants is {{c2::not as tenaciously attached}}.
Specialized ultrasonic tips for implants have {{c1::Teflon-, carbon- or titanium-}}coated shanks, or a removable {{c2::PEEK (polyetheretherketone)}} tip.

basic.front: What is a drawback of the universal curette in areas with tight tissue?
basic.back: It may be difficult to insert/adapt interproximally.
basic.extra: Upside: one instrument can treat all surfaces.

basic.front: Why are subgingival access and adaptation difficult with a hoe?
basic.back: Its bulky working end (which gives it great strength).

typein.question: How many probing measurements are recorded per tooth?
typein.extra: Distofacial, facial, mesiofacial, distolingual, lingual, mesiolingual.

typein.question: How many cutting edges per working end does an area-specific curette have?
typein.extra: The lower/inner cutting edge is used. Sickle scaler: two cutting edges; universal curette: two parallel cutting edges.

typein.question: After Five curette: how many mm longer is its terminal shank than a standard Gracey? (number)
typein.extra: Mini-Five and Micro-Mini Five also have a 3 mm longer terminal shank.

mcq.question: A hygienist needs to detect subgingival calculus in a 7 mm pocket on the distal of #3. Which explorer is the best choice?
mcq.explanation: The #11/12 has a long complex shank with paired working ends for exploring deep periodontal pockets, including posteriors. The pigtail's tip cannot reach deep pockets, and the Orban is mainly for anteriors.

mcq.question: During a periodontal assessment the hygienist suspects Class II furcation involvement on the buccal of #19. Which probe is designed specifically for this assessment?
mcq.explanation: The Naber's probe has curved, paired mirror-image working ends (3 mm intervals) made to enter and assess furcations. The UNC 15 is straight and used for pocket-depth charting, not furcation entry.

mcq.question: A probe with a 0.5 mm ball tip and a colour band from 3.5 to 5.5 mm is used primarily for:
mcq.explanation: That is the WHO probe, used for PSR. Comprehensive charting is done with the UNC 12/15 (bands at 4–5, 9–10, 14–15 mm).

mcq.question: A patient has small, tenacious deposits on the apical third of the mesial root surface of #30 in a 6 mm pocket. Which instrument is most appropriate?
mcq.explanation: Small deposits on the middle or apical third of the root call for an area-specific curette (e.g., Gracey 11/12). A universal curette is for small deposits supragingivally or on the cervical third; sickles and hoes are for supragingival deposits.

mcq.question: While instrumenting with a Gracey curette, the cutting edge is at correct angulation when:
options: A. The face is perpendicular to the tooth
B. The lower shank is tilted toward the tooth
C. The lower shank is parallel to the tooth surface
D. The upper shank is parallel to the long axis
mcq.answer: C. The lower shank is parallel to the tooth surface
mcq.explanation: Gracey (area-specific) faces are offset 60–70° to the lower shank, so a lower shank parallel to the tooth gives correct angulation. Tilting the lower shank toward the tooth is needed for a universal curette (face at 90°).

mcq.question: Which Gracey curette is designed for the distal surfaces of posterior teeth and is NOT used on anterior teeth?
mcq.explanation: Gracey 17/18 is posterior-only, distal surfaces. Gracey 13/14 also reaches posterior distals but is used on anterior mesial/distal surfaces too.

mcq.question: A 7 mm pocket with tight tissue has very tenacious calculus at a narrow furcation entrance. Which curette is the best choice?
mcq.explanation: The Micro-Mini Five has the shortest, narrowest blade and a more rigid shank — made for tenacious calculus, tight tissue and narrow furcations. The After Five has a full-length blade, too long for a narrow furcation.

mcq.question: Which is acceptable during maintenance of a titanium implant?
options: A. Stainless steel Gracey curette with firm lateral pressure
B. Gentle probing with a metal probe
D. A file to smooth the implant surface
mcq.answer: B. Gentle probing with a metal probe
mcq.explanation: The book allows a metal probe used gently; metal scaling instruments should be avoided (use plastic, graphite, coated or titanium instruments, or coated/PEEK ultrasonic tips) with light lateral pressure only.
